claim: Filchenko's consonant table organizes Eastern Khanty consonants across labial, three alveolar articulatory series (apical, dorsal, cacuminal), palatal, and velar places, with stops, glides, fricatives, nasals, laterals and a trill.
/p/ is predominantly voiceless, is most frequent word-initially, can occur with vowels of any quality, and is attested after sonorants.
The bilabial nasal /m/ is palatalized in front-vowel environments.
Both /t/ and /s/ are described as more apical in front-vowel environments and more dorsal in back-vowel environments.
Speakers and earlier studies persistently differentiate alveolar-dental /n/ from alveolar-palatal /n¹/, but Filchenko notes that exact minimal pairs were not attested in his data.

The source's voiced velar/uvular fricative /ƒ/ does not occur preconsonantally and frequently undergoes reductive/assimilative realizations as [q], [k], or [w]; Filchenko nevertheless assumes /ƒ/ underlyingly because it has the widest distribution.

/N/ (the source-encoded dorsal nasal) is velar in front-vowel environments and uvular in back-vowel environments, is excluded word-initially and from syllable onsets, and occasionally reduces/assimilates to /n/ or /k/.

Eastern Khanty maintains phonological differentiation among apical-alveolar, dorsal-palatal and cacuminal-velar articulations, including stop /t/ vs /t’/ and three-way distinctions among laterals and nasals.

Voiced obstruents are not phonemic except /ƒ/. Some idiolects and ideophones show intervocalic or pre-sonorant phonetic voicing, but Filchenko judges the evidence insufficient for a systematic phonological process.

Vowel-triggered assimilation is predominantly palatalization. Most consonants vary allophonically with front/back vowels; front /i e/ are especially strong triggers, and labials /p w m/ plus velar /k/ are especially susceptible.
After /m/, /w/ assimilates to a voiceless bilabial stop in the source's examples.
In the environment of voiceless /t k q tS/, source /ƒ/ yields a voiceless velar or uvular stop /k/ or /q/.

Hiatus between a vowel-final stem and vowel-initial affix is commonly repaired by epenthetic /j/; less frequently /ƒ/ is inserted in a narrowly described imperative environment after coda-less monosyllabic stems ending in a reduced vowel.
At morpheme boundaries, final stops before consonant-initial morphemes are normally articulatorily reduced/lenited and are frequently deleted.

Eastern Khanty strongly avoids consonant clusters. Initial clusters have near-zero frequency and are mostly idiolectal/ideophonic loan pronunciations; typical loan-initial clusters are repaired with an epenthetic reduced central vowel /´/.

Gemination is frequent in derivation/inflection and can result from vowel deletion; /ƒ/-final nominal stems show /ƒ/ replaced by a velar/uvular stop before certain vowel-initial affixes. Filchenko reports no minimal pairs in which consonant length alone differentiates lexemes.

The prose immediately before the formal figure gives basic templates (C)V(C) initially and (CC)V(C) medially/finally, whereas the formal schematic directly below gives (C)V(CC) and C(C)V(CC). This internal source inconsistency must be retained rather than silently reconciled.

Polysyllabic words may carry multiple stresses; primary and secondary stresses are rarely adjacent and are typically separated by one or two syllables, with primary stress usually earlier in the word.
